questions.q: Why does this lesson say a candidate at minute forty still presenting the integration diagram has already lost something, regardless of content quality?
options: Because the panel will fail the candidate automatically at the forty-minute mark
Because integration diagrams are not allowed to be presented after minute thirty
Because they've eaten into the budgeted Q&A time, which needs real room to breathe rather than five rushed minutes at the end
Because Salesforce certification rules require all diagrams to be shown within the first ten minutes
questions.explain: Running long on the walkthrough directly eats into the Q&A period, which is where a design actually gets tested — losing that time costs more than finishing the walkthrough on time would gain.

questions.q: According to this lesson, which diagrams should generally already exist before a live presentation, rather than being drawn from scratch during it?
options: Complex, already-fully-designed diagrams like the data model and integration diagram, since redrawing them live burns time the panel could have seen in seconds on a prepared slide
None — every diagram should be drawn live to show the work
Only diagrams the panel explicitly requests in advance
Only diagrams related to Q&A questions
questions.explain: Pre-drawn artifacts protect walkthrough time; live whiteboarding earns its place specifically for responsive, unplanned explanation, not for redisplaying prepared material.

questions.q: What does "responsive whiteboarding" mean, as distinct from redrawing a prepared diagram?
options: Drawing the exact same diagram twice for emphasis
Asking the panel to draw the diagram themselves
Only drawing diagrams that use a whiteboard app instead of a physical whiteboard
Live drawing used specifically to answer an unplanned Q&A question or build something the panel hasn't already seen, rather than repeating prepared content
questions.explain: Responsive whiteboarding earns its place by showing real-time reasoning on something unplanned — using the same live-drawing time to redisplay a finished diagram doesn't serve that purpose.

questions.q: Why might the security/sharing model artifact earn more walkthrough time than the other three blueprint artifacts in a specific scenario?
options: Because the security/sharing model should always get the most time in every scenario, regardless of content

Because pacing should follow the scenario's actual risk profile, and when the highest-priority risk lives in that domain (as in the Public Sector Case Management scenario), it earns proportionally more time
Because data models and integration diagrams are never important enough to need real time
Because Q&A time should be eliminated whenever security is a major topic
questions.explain: Pacing against the scenario's actual risk profile — not a fixed formula or personal comfort — is what this lesson recommends; a scenario whose biggest risk lives in sharing architecture earns that domain more time.

questions.q: Why does this lesson insist on a stopwatch rehearsal, rather than estimating pacing by reading the outline silently?
options: Because candidates consistently misjudge real spoken pacing in both directions, and only an out-loud, timed rehearsal reveals the actual problem before it costs real session time
Because silent reading and spoken delivery take the same amount of time, so rehearsal is only for memorization
Because stopwatches are a required prop in every official review board
Because rehearsal is only useful for the opening, not the full walkthrough
questions.explain: Guessing pacing from a silent read is unreliable in both directions — underestimating and overestimating are both common — which is why an out-loud, timed rehearsal is the only reliable way to find real pacing issues.
